You could save a little space by only including the lower res versions of textures and models, but I don't think the savings would come to all that much.

The actual program itself wouldn't change very much, since "lower settings" usually means doing less of the same calculations, rather than doing simpler ones. You might eliminate a few specialist shaders, but they don't take up much space.

^ this

The things that take up the most space in any game, on average, are models and textures. Shader files are usually a few kilobytes at most because they're just compiled code for the GPU to process, so there isn't much point in not including them.

Yes.

However, how this could be accomplished would depend on the game and platform. Call of Duty (and a few others I've seen) separate game modes (single player, multiplayer, etc) into different "games" in Steam so you only install what you want.

Another option would to be including different quality assets as free "DLC", only including whats absolutely needed in the base game. This is what Titanfall should have done with it's uncompressed audio. I get why they used uncompressed audio from a technical standpoint, but you shouldn't have to download 6 different languages when most people will only really ever listen to 1. Some games already do this with the highest quality textures as well, but doing this with textures introduces a new level of technical hurdles since a lot of games use the highest-res textures as the base for the rest of the quality settings.

The sad thing is that as nice as smaller install sizes and downloads would be, it is a huge technical hurdle for a relatively small section of the potential install-base.
